text:
Seven games, seven losses, a coach and a goalie under siege, and trade rumors around the best player. Then the Canucks walked into T-Mobile Arena and scored six. It wasn't a performance our numbers would frame (Vegas had 69 shot attempts to 47, 4.19 expected goals to 3.58, and deserved the win in 68% of our replays), but a team in Vancouver's spot doesn't need it to be pretty.

Elias Pettersson, whose name has been in every trade column for two weeks, opened the scoring on the power play at 5:20, a one-timer set up by Jonathan Lekkerimaki and Brock Boeser. Linus Karlsson made it 2-0 on an 8% chance. Victor Olofsson got one back on a Vegas power play, but Filip Chytil, just back in the lineup, tipped in a Boeser shot before the first ended and then scored shorthanded 2:14 into the second, a 36% chance, off Jamie Oleksiak. Chytil's two goals added more to Vancouver's win chances than anyone's.

Vegas owned the second, 1.84 expected goals to 0.96. Braeden Bowman finished a lovely passing play from Dylan Coghlan and William Karlsson, and Mark Stone's power-play goal 1:24 into the third cut it to 4-3 and pulled the Knights' win chance from 11% to 27%. Twenty-four seconds later Drew O'Connor won a faceoff, went to the net and put in a rebound, and that was the night's real turning point. Linus Karlsson's second goal with about two minutes left closed it.

Leevi Merilainen made 34 saves, including the biggest of the night on a Stone chance in the second, and finished 1.2 goals better than expected. Carter Hart was 2.0 goals worse. Stone, to Jesse Granger of The Athletic: "The result for sure shows that. I don't think we managed momentum very well."

One win doesn't change a season that sits at 9 points in 22 games. It does give Manny Malhotra's group something to point to, and Boeser, with two more assists, keeps his point streak going.
headline: Canucks end seven-game skid with six in Vegas
